'''2.''' In ''bot.'' and ''zoöl.'', appearing casually, or in an abnormal or unusual position or place; occurring as a straggler or away from its natural position or habitation; adventive.
{{smaller block|The inflorescence [of ''Cuscata glomerata''] is developed from numerous crowded ''adventitious'' buds, and not by the repeated branching of axillary, flowering branches, as commonly stated. {{right|''Science'', IV. 342.}}}}

'''3.''' In ''anat.'', of the nature of adventitia: as, the ''adventitious'' coat of an artery.

'''adventitiously''' (ad-ven-tish′us-li), ''adv.'' In an adventitious or extrinsic manner; accidentally.

'''adventitiousness''' (ad-ven-tish′us-nes), ''n.'' The state or quality of being adventitious.

'''adventive''' (ad-ven′tiv), ''a.'' and ''n.'' [< L. ''adventus'', pp. of ''advenire'' (see ''advene''), + ''-ive''.] '''I.''' ''a.'' '''1†.''' Accidental; adventitious.
{{smaller block|The relative and ''adventive'' characters of offences. {{right|''Bacon'', Advancement of Learning, ii.}}}}
Specifically—'''2.''' In ''bot.'' and ''zoöl.'', only transient and locally spontaneous, not thoroughly naturalized: applied to introduced plants and animals.

'''II.†''' ''n.'' One who or that which comes from without; an immigrant.
{{smaller block|That the natives be not so many, but that there may be elbow-room enough for them, and for the ''adventives'' also. {{right|''Bacon'', Advice to Villiers.}}}}

'''adventry†''' (ad-ven′tri), ''n.'' [< ''adventure'', as if *''adventury''.] An enterprise; an adventure. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|Act a brave work, call it thy last ''adventry''. {{right|''B. Jonson'', Epigrams.}}}}

'''Adventual''' (ad-ven′tụ̄-al), ''a.'' [< L. as if *''adventualis'', < ''adventus'' (''adventu-''), approach: see ''advent''.] Relating to the season of Advent.

'''adventure''' (ad-ven′tūr), ''n.'' [Early mod. E. often also ''adventer'', < ME. ''aventure'', ''auenture'', often contr. ''auntour'', ''aunter'', ''anter'', etc., < OF. (and F.) ''aventure'' = Pr. Sp. Pg. ''aventura'' = It. ''avventura'' = Fries. ''aventure'' = MHG. ''aventiure'', G. ''abenteuer'' = Dan. ''æventyr'', ''eventyr'' = Sw. ''äfventyr'', < ML. ''aventura'', also ''adventura'', lit. a thing about to happen, < L. ''advenire'', fut. part. act. ''adventurus'', come to, happen: see ''advene''. The ME. prefix ''a''- (''a''-<sup>11</sup>) has been restored to its orig. L. form ''ad''-. Hence ''peradventure'', q. v. Cf. ''venture''.] '''1†.''' That which comes or happens to one; hap; chance; fortune; luck.
{{smaller block|<poem>Searching of thy wound,
I have by hard ''adventure'' found mine own.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', As you Like it, ii. 4.}}
<poem>And as my fair ''adventure'' fell, I found
A lady all in white, with laurel crown’d.</poem>
{{right|''Dryden'', Flower and Leaf, l. 463.}}}}
'''2.''' A hazardous enterprise; an undertaking of uncertain issue, or participation in such an undertaking.
{{smaller block|<poem>He forged,
But that was later, boyish histories
Of battle, bold ''adventure'', dungeon, wreck.</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', Aylmer’s Field.}}}}
'''3.''' A remarkable occurrence in one’s personal history; a noteworthy event or experience in one’s life.

<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|advantage|86|adventuress}}</noinclude>avail (one’s self).

{{smaller block|It is observed of wolves, that when they go to the fold for prey, they will be sure to ''advantage'' themselves of the wind.
{{right|''Rev. T. Adams'', Works, II. 121.}}}}

'''II.''' ''intrans.'' To gain an advantage; be benefited.

{{smaller block|The carnivora ''advantage'' by the accident of their painted skins.
{{right|''P. Robinson'', Under the Sun, p. 185.}}}}

'''advantageable''' (ad-vȧn′tạ̄j-a̤-bl), ''a.'' [Early mod. E. ''avantageable''; < ''advantage'' + ''-able.''] Profitable; convenient; gainful. [Rare.]

{{smaller block|It is ''advantageable'' to a physician to be called to the cure of declining disease.
{{right|''Sir J. Hayward.''}}}}

'''advantage-ground''' (ad-vȧn′tạ̄j-ground), ''n.'' Vantage-ground. ''Clarendon.''

'''advantageous''' (ad-van-tā′jus), ''a.'' [Formerly ''advantagious''; < ''advantage'', ''n.'', + ''-ous'', after F. ''avantageux'', < ''avantage.''] Of advantage; furnishing convenience or opportunity to gain benefit; gainful; profitable; useful; beneficial: as, an ''advantageous'' position of the troops; trade is ''advantageous'' to a nation.

{{smaller block|Between these colonies and the mother country, a very ''advantageous'' traffic was at first carried on.
{{right|''Goldsmith'', Citizen of the World, xxv.}}
It is evident that they [changes in color] are under the control of the fish, and therefore ''advantageous.''
{{right|''Science'', IV. 339.}}}}

{{smaller|=Syn. Helpful, serviceable, favorable, remunerative.}}

'''advantageously''' (ad-van-tā′jus-li), ''adv.'' In an advantageous manner; with advantage; profitably; usefully; conveniently.

{{smaller block|It was ''advantageously'' situated, there being an easy passage from it to India by sea. {{right|''Arbuthnot.''}}
Their mother is evidently not without hopes of seeing one, at least [of her daughters], ''advantageously'' settled in life. {{right|''Barham'', Ingoldsby Legends, I. 184.}}}}

'''advantageousness''' (ad-van-tā′jus-nes), ''n.'' The quality or state of being advantageous; profitableness; usefulness; convenience.
{{smaller block|The last property, which qualifies God for the fittest object of our love, is, the ''advantageousness'' of His to us, both in the present and the future life. {{right|''Boyle'', Works, I. 279.}}}}

'''advectitious''' (ad-vek-tish′us), ''a.'' [< L. ''advectitius'', prop. ''advecticius'', brought to a place from a distance, foreign, < ''advectus'', pp. of ''advehere'', bring to: see ''advehent.''] Brought from another place. ''Blount.''

'''advehent''' (ad′vē-hent), ''a.'' [< L. ''advehen(t-)s'', ppr. of ''advehere'', bring to, carry to, < ''ad'', to, + ''vehere'', bring, carry: see ''vehicle'', ''convey.''] Bringing; carrying to; afferent: in ''anat.'', applied to sundry vessels: the opposite of ''revehent.''

'''advene''' (ad-vēn′), ''v. i.'' [< L. ''advenire'', come to, arrive at, < ''ad'', to, + ''venire'', come, = E. ''come'', q. v. Cf. ''convene'', ''intervene'', ''supervene.''] To accede or come; be added or become a part, though not essential. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|Where no act of the will ''advenes'' as a co-efficient. {{right|''Coleridge'', Remains (1836), III. 19.}}}}

'''advenient†''' (ad-vē′nient), ''a.'' [< L. ''advenien(t-)s'', ppr. of ''advenire:'' see ''advene.''] Advening; coming from without; superadded.
{{smaller block|Divided from truth in themselves, they are yet farther removed by ''advenient'' deception. {{right|''Sir T. Browne'', Vulg. Err., i. 3.}}}}

'''advent''' (ad′vent), ''n.'' [< ME. ''advent'', < L. ''adventus'', a coming to, approach, < ''advenire'': see ''advene''.] '''1.''' A coming into place, view, or being; visitation; arrival; accession: as, the ''advent'' of visitors, of an infant, or of death. [A modern use of the word, the ecclesiastical use having been the original one in English.]
{{smaller block|With the ''advent'' of the empire all this was destined to undergo a complete change.
{{right|''Merivale'', Roman Empire, xxxv.}}
With the ''advent'' to power of a liberal-minded Sovereign . . . it might have been expected that there would be an immediate change in the Government of Piedmont.
{{right|''E. Dicey'', Victor Emmanuel, p. 54.}}}}
Specifically—'''2.''' The coming of Christ as the Saviour of the world. Hence—'''3.''' [''cap.''] ''Eccles.'', the period immediately preceding the festival of the Nativity. {{smaller|It includes four Sundays, reckoning from the Sunday nearest St. Andrew’s day (Nov. 30) to Christmas eve, and has been observed since the sixth century as a season of devotion with reference to the coming of Christ in the flesh and to his second coming to judge the world; in the Roman Catholic Church observed also as a time of penance and fasting. In the Oriental and Greek Churches the period includes six Sundays, or forty days.—'''Second advent,''' the second coming of Christ to establish a personal reign upon the earth as its king. See ''millenarianism'' and ''premillennialism''.}}

'''Adventist''' (ad′ven-tist), ''n.'' [< ''advent'' + ''-ist''.] One who believes in the second coming of Christ to establish a personal reign upon the earth; a millenarian; a Second-adventist. {{smaller|The Adventists of the United States owe their origin to the millenarian teachings of William Miller (see ''Millerite''), most of them believing at first in various dates fixed for the second coming of Christ from 1843 to 1861, but aftercipal of which are: the ''Advent'' (or ''Second Advent'') ''Christians'', the largest; the ''Seventh-day Adventists'', much smaller, but more compactly organized; and the ''Evangelical Adventists'', the smallest. The members of the first two believe in the final annihilation of the wicked, which those of the third reject. The second observe the seventh day as the Sabbath, and believe in the existence of the spirit of prophecy among them; they maintain missions in various parts of the world, and a number of institutions at Battle Creek, Michigan, their headquarters.}}

'''adventitia''' (ad-ven-tish′i-ä), ''n.'' [NL., fem. sing. (sc. ''membrana'', or ''tunica'') of L. ''adventitius'': see ''adventitious''.] In ''anat.'', any membranous structure covering an organ but not properly belonging to it (in full, ''membrana adventitia'', adventitious membrane); specifically, the outermost of the three coats of a blood-vessel (in full, ''tunica adventitia'', adventitious tunic), consisting of connective tissue.

'''adventitious''' (ad-ven-tish′us), ''a.'' [< L. ''adventitius'', prop. ''adventicius'', coming from abroad, < ''adventus'', pp. of ''advenire'': see ''advene''.] '''1.''' Added extrinsically; not springing from the essence of the subject, but from another source; foreign; accidentally or casually acquired: applied to that which does not properly belong to a subject, but which is superadded or adopted, as in a picture or other work of art, to give it additional power or effect.
{{smaller block|Every subject acquires an ''adventitious'' importance to him who considers it with application.
{{right|''Goldsmith'', Polite Learning, xiv.}}
But apart from any ''adventitious'' associations of later growth, it is certain that a very ancient belief gave to magic the power of imparting life, or the semblance of it, to inanimate things.
{{right|''Lowell'', Among my Books, 1st ser., p. 117.}}}}

'''2.''' In ''bot.'' and ''zoöl.'', appearing casually, or in an abnormal or unusual position or place; occurring as a straggler or away from its natural position or habitation; adventive.
{{smaller block|The inflorescence [of ''Cuscata glomerata''] is developed from numerous crowded ''adventitious'' buds, and not by the repeated branching of axillary, flowering branches, as commonly stated. {{right|''Science'', IV. 342.}}}}

'''3.''' In ''anat.'', of the nature of adventitia: as, the ''adventitious'' coat of an artery.

'''adventitiously''' (ad-ven-tish′us-li), ''adv.'' In an adventitious or extrinsic manner; accidentally.

'''adventitiousness''' (ad-ven-tish′us-nes), ''n.'' The state or quality of being adventitious.

'''adventive''' (ad-ven′tiv), ''a.'' and ''n.'' [< L. ''adventus'', pp. of ''advenire'' (see ''advene''), + ''-ive''.] '''I.''' ''a.'' '''1†.''' Accidental; adventitious.
{{smaller block|The relative and ''adventive'' characters of offences. {{right|''Bacon'', Advancement of Learning, ii.}}}}
Specifically—'''2.''' In ''bot.'' and ''zoöl.'', only transient and locally spontaneous, not thoroughly naturalized: applied to introduced plants and animals.

'''II.†''' ''n.'' One who or that which comes from without; an immigrant.
{{smaller block|That the natives be not so many, but that there may be elbow-room enough for them, and for the ''adventives'' also. {{right|''Bacon'', Advice to Villiers.}}}}

'''adventry†''' (ad-ven′tri), ''n.'' [< ''adventure'', as if *''adventury''.] An enterprise; an adventure. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|Act a brave work, call it thy last ''adventry''. {{right|''B. Jonson'', Epigrams.}}}}

'''Adventual''' (ad-ven′tụ̄-al), ''a.'' [< L. as if *''adventualis'', < ''adventus'' (''adventu-''), approach: see ''advent''.] Relating to the season of Advent. {{smaller block|{{right|''Bp. Sanderson.''}}}}

'''adventure''' (ad-ven′tūr), ''n.'' [Early mod. E. often also ''adventer'', < ME. ''aventure'', ''auenture'', often contr. ''auntour'', ''aunter'', ''anter'', etc., < OF. (and F.) ''aventure'' = Pr. Sp. Pg. ''aventura'' = It. ''avventura'' = Fries. ''aventure'' = MHG. ''aventiure'', G. ''abenteuer'' = Dan. ''æventyr'', ''eventyr'' = Sw. ''äfventyr'', < ML. ''aventura'', also ''adventura'', lit. a thing about to happen, < L. ''advenire'', fut. part. act. ''adventurus'', come to, happen: see ''advene''. The ME. prefix ''a''- (''a''-<sup>11</sup>) has been restored to its orig. L. form ''ad''-. Hence ''peradventure'', q. v. Cf. ''venture''.] '''1†.''' That which comes or happens to one; hap; chance; fortune; luck.
{{smaller block|<poem>Searching of thy wound,
I have by hard ''adventure'' found mine own.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', As you Like it, ii. 4.}}
<poem>And as my fair ''adventure'' fell, I found
A lady all in white, with laurel crown’d.</poem>
{{right|''Dryden'', Flower and Leaf, l. 463.}}}}
'''2.''' A hazardous enterprise; an undertaking of uncertain issue, or participation in such an undertaking.
{{smaller block|<poem>He forged,
But that was later, boyish histories
Of battle, bold ''adventure'', dungeon, wreck.</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', Aylmer’s Field.}}}}
'''3.''' A remarkable occurrence in one’s personal history; a noteworthy event or experience in one’s life.

'''4.''' A speculation of any kind, commercial, financial, or mining; a venture; specifically, a speculation in goods sent abroad.
{{smaller block|Lafayette directed the captain to steer for the United States, which, especially as he had a large pecuniary ''adventure'' of his own on board, he declined doing.
{{right|''Everett'', Orations, I. 467.}}}}

'''5†.''' Peril; danger.
{{smaller block|He was in great ''adventure'' of his life. {{right|''Berners''.}}}}

'''6.''' Adventurous activity; participation in exciting or hazardous undertakings or enterprises: as, a spirit of ''adventure''.—{{smaller|'''At all adventures'''†, at all hazards; whatever may be the consequence.}}
{{smaller block|In this mist ''at all adventures'' go. {{right|''Shak.'', C. of E., ii. 2.}}}}
{{smaller|'''Bill of adventure.''' See ''bill''<sup>3</sup>.}}

'''adventure''' (ad-ven′t̮ūr), ''v.''; pret. and pp. ''adventured'', ppr. ''adventuring''. [< ME. ''aventuren'', usually contr. to ''aunteren'', ''auntren'' (which survives, prob., in ''saunter'', q. v.), < OF. ''aventurer'' = Pr. Sp. Pg. ''aventurar'' = It. ''avventurare'', < ML. ''adventurare''; from the noun.] '''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To risk or hazard; put in the power of unforeseen events: as, to ''adventure'' one’s life.
{{smaller block|My father fought for you, and ''adventured'' his life far.
{{right|Judges ix. 17.}}}}

'''2.''' To venture on; take the chance of; run the risk of doing or suffering.
{{smaller block|<poem>So bold Leander would ''adventure'' it.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', T. G. of V., iii. 1.}}
<poem>Well, my lord, I do ''adventure'', on your word,
The duke’s displeasure.</poem>
{{right|''Dekker and Webster''(?), Sir Thomas Wyat, p. 15.}}}}

'''II.''' ''intrans.'' To take the risk involved in doing anything; proceed at a venture.

{{smaller block|Still y<sup>e</sup> plague continuing in our parish, I could not without danger ''adventure'' to our church.
{{right|''Evelyn'', Diary, Sept. 7, 1666.}}}}
{{smaller block|Its government began to ''adventure'' on a lenient policy.
{{right|''Bancroft'', Hist. U. S., I. 349.}}}}

'''adventureful''' (ad-ven′t̮ūr-fu̇l), ''a.'' Given to adventure; full of enterprise. [Rare.]

'''adventurement†''' (ad-ven′t̮ūr-mẹnt), ''n.'' Hazardous enterprise.
{{smaller block|<poem>Wiser Raymundus, in his closet pent,
Laughs at such danger and ''adventurement.''</poem>
{{right|''Bp. Hall'', Satires, IV. iii. 35.}}}}

'''adventurer''' (ad-ven′t̮ūr-ėr), ''n.'' [Late ME. ''adventorer'', a gamester, suggested by F. ''aventurier'', with same sense, < ML. ''adventurarius'', ''-erius'': see ''adventure'' and ''-er''.] '''1.''' One who engages in adventure; an undertaker of uncertain or hazardous actions or enterprises, as in travel, war, trade, speculation, etc.: as, the Young ''Adventurer'', a title given to Prince Charles Edward Stuart on account of his leading the desperate insurrection of 1745. {{smaller|Specifically—(''a'') One of a class of soldiers in the middle ages who sold their services to the highest bidder, or fought and plundered on their own account. (''b'') Formerly, a seeker of fortune by foreign trade, travel, or emigration; one who engaged in foreign discovery, colonization, or speculation for the sake of profit, especially in North America.}}
{{smaller block|While these things were thus acting in America, the ''adventurers'' in England were providing, though too tediously, to send them recruits.
{{right|''Beverley'', Virginia, i. ¶ 7.}}}}
{{smaller block|The [colonial] governor [of Maryland] was authorized to erect each holding of 1,000 acres and over into a manor, to}}

{{smaller block|be called by such name as the ''adventurer'' or ''adventurers'' shall desire.
{{right|''Johns Hopkins Univ. Stud.'', III. 319.}}}}

{{smaller|(''c'') In general, one who undertakes any great commercial risk or speculation; a speculator; in ''mining'', a shareholder in or promoter of mines, particularly under the cost-book system. See ''cost-book''.}}

'''2.''' In a bad sense, a seeker of fortune by underhand or equivocal means; a speculator upon the credulity or good nature of others; especially, one who ingratiates himself with society by false show or pretense in order to gain a surreptitious livelihood.—'''Adventurer tunnel.''' {{smaller|See ''tunnel''.—'''Merchant Adventurers,''' the title of a commercial company first established in Antwerp, and chartered in England by Henry IV. in 1406, and by successive sovereigns down to Charles I. in 1634, who carried on trading and colonizing enterprises in North America and other parts of the world. Several local associations of merchants still exist in England under this name, that of Newcastle reckoning its origin from the seventeenth year of King John (1216).}}

'''adventuresome''' (ad-ven′t̮ūr-sum), ''a.'' [< ''adventure'', ''n.'', + ''-some''.] Bold; daring; adventurous; incurring hazard. See ''venturesome''.
{{smaller block|<poem>''Adventuresome'', I send
My herald thought into a wilderness.</poem>
{{right|''Keats'', Endymion, i.}}}}

'''adventuresomeness''' (ad-ven′t̮ūr-sum-nes), ''n.'' The quality of being bold and venturesome.

'''adventuress''' (ad-ven′t̮ūr-es), ''n.'' [< ''adventurer'' + ''-ess''.] A female adventurer; a woman engaged in or capable of bold enterprises, especially enterprises of equivocal character.<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
